help.heading: How to use the recipe calculator
help.intro: The calculator turns a glaze recipe, the weights of the raw materials you mix, into its unity molecular formula: the oxides the glaze becomes in the kiln, scaled so the fluxes add up to 1. It updates as you type.

name.heading: Name the recipe
name.text: Give it a title. The date and notes are optional; notes are a good place for the cone, the atmosphere and how the test came out.

materials.heading: Add the materials
materials.text: Under Add materials, choose My materials (the ones you entered on the Materials page, such as your own analysis of a feldspar) or Standard (the built-in list). Type part of a name in the filter to narrow a long list, then click a material to add it. The cursor moves to its amount.

amounts.heading: Enter the amounts
amounts.text: Use any unit: percent, parts or grams. Only the proportions matter to the chemistry. The share column shows each material's percent of the batch, and the total is under the list.

unity.heading: Read the unity formula
unity.text: It sits beside the recipe (below it on a phone) and changes with every amount you type:
unity.fluxes: Fluxes (R₂O and RO) add up to 1.000; they make the glaze melt.
unity.stabilizers: Stabilizers (R₂O₃), mainly alumina, stiffen the melt so it stays on the pot.
unity.glassFormers: Glass formers (RO₂), mainly silica, make the glass.
unity.ratio: The silica to alumina ratio hints at the surface: higher ratios tend to be glossier, lower ones more matte, though the fluxes and the firing matter too.
unity.problems: If a material is unknown, an amount is not a number, or nothing in the recipe is a flux, it says so.

additives.heading: Add colorants and additives
additives.text: These go on top of the base. They are saved with the recipe but are not part of the unity formula. Choose what each amount is in:
additives.percent: % of base: a percent of the base's total, as most recipes give them: 2 means 2% red iron oxide.
additives.parts: parts: the same unit as the materials, such as 1 part on a base of 3 flint and 2 dolomite.
additives.grams: grams: a weight, in the same batch as the materials.
additives.count: Some calculators count colorants in the unity formula and some do not. Tick Count colorants and additives in it, under the Unity formula heading, to count them at their weight in the batch, or leave it clear to compare with one that does not. The choice is saved with the recipe.

scale.heading: Change the scale when you need to
scale.percent: To percent: the materials add up to 100.
scale.parts: To parts: the smallest whole numbers that fit, such as 3 flint and 2 dolomite; a material that does not divide evenly keeps its exact amount, such as 1.477.
scale.batch: Scale to a batch: enter a weight, such as 500 g, to get the grams to weigh out. With weights in pounds and ounces (under Settings on your account page), enter pounds, such as 12.5: the amounts become pounds, each shown in pounds and ounces under it.
scale.text: Every amount changes at once, to up to five decimal places, and the unity formula stays the same. Colorants in parts or grams change with the materials; those in % of base stay as they are, since a percent of the base is the same at any scale.

save.heading: Save
save.save: Save keeps the recipe here and adds it to My saved recipes. Saving again updates that same recipe.
save.next: Save and add next recipe saves, then clears the page for the next one.
save.copy: Save as a copy saves your changes as a new recipe and leaves the original as it was: good for variations on a recipe.
save.open: Open, in My saved recipes, brings a saved recipe back here to change it.

compare.heading: Compare two recipes
compare.text: Compare, beside Save or on a saved recipe, lines up two unity formulas oxide by oxide, with the change from the first to the second. To compare like with like, count the colorants in both or in neither.
compare.modern: A recipe that uses a material no longer made, such as Custer Spar, says what is used now, and whether it can take its place gram for gram. Try modern materials and compare swaps them in, one for one, as a new recipe, and compares it with the old one; Undo the swap puts it back. Where a swap is not like for like, Suggest amounts and compare works the amounts out again to bring the unity formula back, changing as few as it can. If the new material cannot bring back something the old one gave, such as niter's potash, it asks what should. It matches the fired oxides only, so test a small batch first.
compare.lead: A recipe with lead says so. Replace lead asks the cone you fire to and which lead-free frit to build on, then either rebuilds the glaze (its silica and alumina kept, with boron and other fluxes doing lead's work) or keeps its colorants on a lead-free base of the frit and kaolin, 85 to 15. Materials with lead are listed to add only when lead is on under Settings on your account page.
compare.shelf: Match with what I have makes the recipe again from only the materials you have on hand, as near its fired oxides as they allow. Your list of materials on hand is kept with your account.
compare.tries: Each of these can take materials to try, any you have or would like considered, and tick Must use to keep one in. The new recipe says what each material supplies and whether the match needs it, what else would help, and what to watch for. Past a recommended limit, such as a lot of boron at cone 6 or raw whiting at cone 04, it says what the glaze will likely do rather than refuse. Its buttons work the recipe out again from the old one: leave a material out, add one, or allow more past a limit.

numbers.heading: Read the analysis and the limits
numbers.analysis: Analysis and limits, under the recipe, shows each oxide's moles, mole % and fired weight %, the loss on ignition and the calculated thermal expansion, an estimate for comparing glazes.
numbers.limits: Limits sets the unity formula against a limit set: Hesselberth & Roy's stable glaze limits unless you choose Glazecalc's own (the choice is saved with your settings). It checks the firing band the recipe's Firing gives: its cone, or its range. A range that crosses bands, such as cone 6 to 10, shows both bands' checks side by side. To check one band only, choose it in the limits' own Firing box, which overrides the recipe's firing and is saved with the recipe. Hesselberth & Roy's figures are for cone 6 and cone 10, so at low fire it says they do not apply. They are guidelines, not a pass or a fail. At the top, one line compares the glaze's boron, silica and alumina with its firing, by Katz's boron rule and Hesselberth & Roy's figures whichever limit set you choose: it gives a note only when they agree that the glaze looks like a different firing, says when it can't judge (lead, lithium, raku and the like), and is a guide, not a test.
numbers.stull: The Stull chart plots the glaze's silica against its alumina, with Stull's matte, semi-matte and bright regions and the limit set's ranges. It is a guide to the surface, not a prediction.
numbers.slurry: Specific gravity and water uses Brongniart's formula: weigh a measured volume of the glaze, then see the dry glaze in the bucket, the water that brings it to the SG you want, or the water for a new batch. Densities follow your setting for specific gravity, Baumé or pint weight.

print.heading: Print it for the glaze room
print.text: Print, beside Save or on a saved recipe, lays it out for paper. Print the whole recipe with its unity formula and analysis, or just a batch list: what to weigh for a batch of any size, a running total for weighing into one bucket, and boxes to tick. Weights are in grams, to a tenth or in full, or in pounds and ounces: choose under Settings on your account page.

help.tips: Tips: a material that is not in the standard list can be added on the Materials page from its chemical formula or the supplier's analysis. And test before you trust: the numbers show tendencies, not what your kiln will do.

hazards.heading: Hazards
hazards.intro: As each material's record gives them; the standard library's come from the suppliers' safety data sheets.
hazards.unknown: {count, plural, one {No hazards are given for {list}: see the safety data sheet that comes with it.} other {No hazards are given for {list}: see the safety data sheets that come with them.}}
hazards.safety: Dry glaze materials make dust, and you must keep it out of your lungs, even dust from materials not classified as hazardous. See <mixing>Safe mixing and ventilation</mixing>, and <home>Don't poison your family</home> if children or pets are about. Where a material's safety data sheet says more, follow it.

why.rawCalcium: this app's own guideline for raw whiting and dolomite at low fire, where they barely melt and give off gas
why.lowExpansion: low-expansion frits are craze cures, used at about 5 to 10%
why.boronFrit: a calcium borate frit is a boron top-up, not a base
why.zinc: raw zinc oxide's melting power drops quickly above about 5%, and it can crawl

lead.baseDoingLittle: The match uses only {percent}% of {base}: at this firing the other materials do most of the melting, so the choice of base frit matters little here.
lead.antimony: Antimony gives Naples yellow only with lead: without it the yellow will not form. Use a commercial yellow stain rated for your cone.
lead.chrome: Red, orange or yellow from chrome comes from lead; without it chrome turns green. Use a stain rated for your cone for those colours.
lead.copper: Copper turns bluer, toward turquoise, without lead.
lead.manganese: Manganese turns plum or violet rather than brown.
lead.iron: An iron honey glaze is less warm without lead, and can turn olive.

checks.boronLowFire: This has more boron ({boron}) than most cone 06-04 glazes.
checks.boronLowFireProbably: It will probably melt early and run, so leave a wider foot.
checks.boronLowFireTends: It tends to melt early and run, so leave a wider foot.
checks.boronLowFireEffects: It may pinhole or blister, turn milky blue-white where thick, and wear less well. More kaolin and silica steady it.
checks.boronMidFire: This is a lot of boron for cone 6 ({boron}; industry counts {high} as high).
checks.boronMidFireSet: This is a lot of boron for cone 6 ({boron}; this limit set counts {high} as high).
checks.boronHighFire: This is a lot of boron for cone 10 ({boron}; this limit set counts {high} as high).
checks.boronMidFireProbably: Glazes like this will probably run, go milky or streaky, and may craze or wear less well.
checks.boronMidFireTends: Glazes like this tend to run, go milky or streaky, and may craze or wear less well.
checks.boronMidFireFix: Use just enough boron to melt; kaolin and silica steady it.
checks.boronShort: This has less boron ({boron}) than glazes usually need at this firing (about {needed}).
checks.boronShortEffects: It may not melt fully, coming out stiff, dry or pinholed. Test it; if it is underfired, a hotter firing or a little more base frit helps.
checks.aluminaLow: There is very little alumina here ({alumina}).
checks.aluminaLowProbably: It will probably be a glossy glaze that runs, may grow crystals or cloud as it cools, and is softer and less durable.
checks.aluminaLowTends: It tends to be a glossy glaze that runs, may grow crystals or cloud as it cools, and is softer and less durable.
checks.aluminaLowFix: More kaolin, or a frit with more alumina, usually fixes it.
checks.aluminaHigh: There is a lot of alumina for the silica (silica to alumina {ratio}:1).
checks.aluminaHighEffects: It may not melt fully and can come out dry or matte, with pinholes or bare patches.
checks.aluminaHighLowFire: At cone 06-02 a matte like this is often under-melted, so test it before using it for food.
checks.aluminaHighFix: More flux or less kaolin brings back the gloss.
checks.boronBlue: Lots of calcium with lots of boron tends to go milky blue-white where the glaze pools ("boron blue").
checks.boronBlueFixPink: More kaolin or faster cooling usually clears it.
checks.boronBlueFix: Less calcium, more kaolin or faster cooling usually clears it.
checks.alkali: This has a lot of soda and potash ({alkali}). Colours will be bright (copper turns turquoise).
checks.alkaliProbably: But it will probably craze, sometimes weeks later, and has a softer surface that can leach: fine for decorative pieces, not for food surfaces.
checks.alkaliTends: But it tends to craze, sometimes weeks later, and has a softer surface that can leach: fine for decorative pieces, not for food surfaces.
checks.alkaliFix: Trading some for calcium, magnesium, boron or lithium reduces crazing.
checks.magnesia: Magnesia ({magnesia}) does not melt at cone 06-04.
checks.magnesiaProbably: It will probably make the glaze stiffer, more matte and opaque, and can make it crawl.
checks.magnesiaTends: It tends to make the glaze stiffer, more matte and opaque, and can make it crawl.
checks.magnesiaNote: It mutes chrome-tin pinks, though it does help against crazing.
checks.zincChrome: Zinc turns chrome greens brown and spoils chrome-tin pinks; Mason says no zinc with these stains. Leave the zinc out, or use a stain made for zinc glazes.
checks.zincIron: Zinc can muddy iron colours. For clean ambers and honey browns, test a version without zinc.
checks.zincCopper: Zinc shifts copper colour, often bluer or brighter rather than green. Test before relying on it.
checks.zincLowFire: Below about cone 03, zinc ({zinc}) does little melting. It may crawl or pinhole and give a matte or crystal surface; calcined zinc crawls less.
checks.whiting: Whiting barely melts at cone 06-04 and gives off gas as it breaks down.
checks.whitingProbably: At {percent}% it will probably pinhole or blister and come out dry, matte or chalky.
checks.whitingTends: At {percent}% it tends to pinhole or blister and come out dry, matte or chalky.
checks.whitingFix: Calcium from a frit or from wollastonite avoids both. (5% is this app's guideline; no published limit gives one.)
checks.fluorine: {name} releases fluorine as it fires. Vent the kiln well, or use a material without fluorine in its place.
checks.clayLowWas: This has only {clay}% raw clay; the old recipe had {was}%.
checks.clayNoneWas: This has no raw clay; the old recipe had {was}%.
checks.clayLowFix: Without clay a glaze settles hard in the bucket and dusts off the pot before firing. Add 1-2% bentonite to keep it suspended, or keep some clay and accept a slightly different match.
checks.clayHigh: Over 20% raw clay ({clay}%) shrinks a lot as the glaze dries.
checks.clayHighProbably: It will probably crack on the pot and crawl into bare patches in the kiln.
checks.clayHighTends: It tends to crack on the pot and crawl into bare patches in the kiln.
checks.clayHighFix: Swap part of it for calcined kaolin (about 12% less by weight), keeping about 15-20% raw so the glaze stays suspended.
checks.soluble: {name} dissolves in water, which makes it a poor glaze material: it soaks into the pot and changes as the glaze stands. Frits carry the same oxides without dissolving.
checks.boronFrit: A calcium borate frit is normally a small boron top-up, not a base (one seller says 10% at most). As the main frit, expect a runny glaze that may turn milky or blue-white and grow crystals in the bucket. Use a borosilicate base frit and keep this one small.
checks.lowExpansionFrit: Low-expansion frits are craze cures, used at about 5-10%. As the main frit the glaze may not melt fully at cone 06-02 and can look dull; where it does melt, it may shiver, throwing sharp flakes off rims.
checks.alkaliFrit: A high-alkaline frit as the main flux gives bright colour but a soft, fluid glaze that crazes on almost any clay: good for crackle and raku, not for food surfaces.
checks.expansionRises: Its calculated expansion rises from {was} to {now}.
checks.expansionRisesProbably: If the old glaze only just fitted your clay, this one will probably craze, sometimes weeks later.
checks.expansionRisesMay: If the old glaze only just fitted your clay, this one may craze, sometimes weeks later.
checks.expansionRisesFix: Crazing weakens pots and is not advised on food surfaces. Swapping some soda and potash for lower-expansion fluxes (boron, lithium, magnesium or calcium) lowers the thermal expansion; adding silica is sometimes suggested, but sources disagree.
checks.expansionFalls: Its calculated expansion falls from {was} to {now}. A little lower usually resists crazing better.
checks.expansionFallsProbably: Much lower will probably shiver, with sharp flakes off rims and edges.
checks.expansionFallsCan: Much lower can shiver, with sharp flakes off rims and edges.
checks.expansionFallsTest: Test it on your own clay.
checks.manyMaterials: This recipe has {count, plural, one {# base material} other {# base materials}}. Most published glazes have 4 to 6, and fewer than 1 in 25 have 8 or more; each one is another material to buy, store and weigh.
checks.smallAmount: {name} is {percent}% of the batch, {percent} g in a 100 g test: weigh it on a scale that reads {reads} g or better, or leave it out.

why.rawClay: raw clay shrinks as the glaze dries, and much of it can crack on the pot and crawl in the kiln; calcined kaolin can make up the rest

numbers.heading: Analysis and limits
numbers.caption: The glaze's oxides
numbers.captionCounted: The glaze's oxides, counting colorants and additives
numbers.moleNote: Unity is the formula with the fluxes adding up to 1; mole % is each oxide's share of all the molecules; weight % is its share of the fired glaze by weight.
numbers.expansionNote: The expansion is an estimate for comparing glazes, not a measured value: each fired oxide's weight percent times its coefficient, with Digitalfire's coefficients (which Glazy uses too, after West and Gerrow). Which way it moves from one glaze to another is surer than by how much.

limits.heading: Limits

notes.hesselberth-roy: John Hesselberth and Ron Roy's recommended limits for stable glazes on functional stoneware and porcelain, at cone 6 and cone 10. They keep to a short list of materials, so the set has no range for barium or lithium, nor for zinc at cone 10.
notes.glazecalc: The figures the app warns at when it swaps materials: boron, alumina, soda and potash, and magnesia at low fire.

slurry.heading: Specific gravity and water
slurry.intro: Weigh a measured volume of the glaze to find its specific gravity (SG), then see what the bucket holds, the water that brings it to the SG you want, or the water for a new batch. It uses Brongniart's formula.

slurry.note: The water is by weight: a litre weighs a kilogram, a US gallon about 8.3 lb. The arithmetic takes the volumes to add, which is close, not exact: add water a little at a time, stir, and measure again. Two glazes at the same SG can still flow differently.

worked.heading: How the unity formula is worked out
worked.intro: The unity (Seger) formula gives a glaze as moles of each oxide, scaled so that its fluxes add up to 1. Here are the steps, with this recipe's numbers; Glazecalc works its own out the same way.
worked.gramsText: Read each amount as grams of the material. Any batch size gives the same unity formula, since every number is divided by the fluxes' total in the end.
worked.molesHeading: Find the moles of each oxide in each material
worked.molesText: A material's analysis gives the percent of each oxide it leaves after firing. Its grams × that percent ÷ 100 are the grams of the oxide, and those grams ÷ the oxide's molar mass (the grams in one mole of it) are its moles.
worked.loi: Loss on ignition {loi}%: water and carbon dioxide that burn away and leave no oxide.
worked.totalsHeading: Add up the moles of each oxide
worked.totalsText: Add each oxide's moles from every material. The fluxes, which melt the glass, are the R₂O and RO oxides, such as soda, potash, lime and magnesia.
worked.divideHeading: Divide every oxide by the fluxes' total
worked.divideText: Divide each oxide's moles by {total}, the fluxes' total. Then the fluxes add up to 1, and each other oxide is in moles for each mole of flux.
worked.answerText: The same numbers as potters read them: fluxes, stabilizers and glass formers, with the silica to alumina ratio.
worked.rounding: The numbers are rounded to show them, but each step uses them unrounded, so adding up the rounded figures can be off in the last place.
worked.noAmounts: There is nothing to work out: the materials have no amounts.

help.cone: The cone you fired this glaze to. Cones measure heatwork (time and temperature), not just temperature, so cone 06 is much cooler than cone 6.
help.range: If it works over a range, give the lowest and highest cone, and tick the cones you have actually fired it to: the tested cone shows first. A glaze can look, and behave, differently at each end.
help.convert: The cone is kept as you give it. Any conversion to another scale or to a temperature is approximate: a cone bends at a different temperature at a different heating rate, and SK and Orton cones with the same number are not the same.
help.move: Moving a glaze to another cone usually means reformulating it, not just firing it hotter or cooler. Duplicate for another cone keeps both versions.
